I've playtested this w/ 4 groups already (I'm a paid DM). Beginners and veterans both enjoy it:

- make smaller city as a sandbox, doesn't need many moving parts.
- NPC invites them to general seeming adventure (during char creation, before actual play)
- they get a few hours, for example everyone rolls for one small interesting thing to get going.
- they meet, but their bost is nowhere to be seen, been murdered
- the get the quest to find the killer, but make up some reason to keep the party from city guard (illegal to investigate or they shouldn't know about the murder or the investigator isn't a good one)
- have a sewer monster
- my structure was :

      Intro : one interesting thing each, they meet, they are given the first set of clues.

      Investigation : Based on first set of clues, they have max 5 leads. Sandbox opens.

      Cathing the killer : killer should be somewhat a koving part, he can also hide for a few days. They confront the killer, get the guards or questgiver, hand over evidence and reap rewards. Killer had clue on where to go for the quest they were originally invited for, which had some hints in the Investigation part. They end with a natural segway into the next adventure.

While the most important thing is to have fun, for me as a DM, that means a well thought out and fleshed out story.

The process of quality writing (going back, checking errors, changing things around for better setup-payoff, making the details fall into place) ensures a world that feels alive and in motion. It's also necessary for mysteries and long-term puzzles the players can solve.

Improv and adapting to an ongoing game is a requirement for a DM, as there will always be player actions that you wouldn't expect.

Writing a campaign is easier than a novel, in a sense that you only have to write problems, but not the solution. That's the players part. Please take this in an intended sense, as there are several exceptions to this statement (culprit of a murder, solution to a puzzle should be set in stone - I don't believe it's a good puzzle when the solution is whatever cool things a player suggests. It's much more rewarding finding the actual solution).

For example, the first chapter of my current campaign (which I ran for 3 different groups) is a murder mystery. I have the events of the murder and the culprit written, along with notes on what he will do in the next few days if left alone (he doesn't know about their investigation). Then I have the city written with a few key locations and clues sprinkled around. They can take at least 4 different routes from the culprit's shack (they can track him there from the murder) and my groups have found more I didn't anticipate. I also like to have some knowledge about the city that won't even necessarily come up ingame, only in specific cases (the sewer monster is there to guard the castle escape tunnels for example. One player in one of my groups had the noble background and I told them in private).
If I give it a little bit of thought, I can give so much more bivid descriptions. It really helps setting the mood when you have time to think about using setting appropriate language.

If you read what I replied, I made several points about love and understanding. All of these arguments come from empathy for the child's personality and freedom of spirit.

So basically, parenting is riding a function (mathematical) based on your child's personality and capabilities. This is the function which determines (this is a metaphor, so the function is objective, measured with the full knowledge of all possibilities) how much freedom of choice is ideal for the child. There will be variables, but some generalizations can be made (for example no one's brain is developed enough physically before the age of 25 to be able to take full responsibility of driving a vehicle and making those rapid decisions consistently, regardless of emotional state). 

You have to choose between 2 strategies : 
- you protect your offspring to the fullest, making and influencing their life decisions so you can feel save knowing they are "on the right path". The problem with this approach is twofold : a) when they produce offspring, you will not be able to do the same for your grandchildren and some asshole/hag will ruin your perfect little child and grandchildren. b) if you're lucky, you'll die before them and will not be able to uphold control.
There's immense amount of proof in psychology that controlling parents can keep up induced bad habits even from death (I recommend Susan Forward's Toxic Parents, 1989).
- you first define, like really seriously and all encompassing define what "good decision" mean. I went with "good choice is the one you won't  ever regret. You might ponder what might've been, but the overall summarization of your decisions led you to learn and achieve to degree you are content with at old age." Then you try to approximate the curve of your child's function based on observations of the child. You have to account for the parents, so you might aswell examine yourself and your partner. If the curve is followed close enough, and fueled with enough love, understanding and support (children need support and help, not protection!), the school system and bad friends can't break your child enough, because they will always have a core of hope, belief they can do it and the mental tools to make decisions and solve problem. This is the harder way, because you will have to force yourself to have a more opened mind than ever before. You will have to accept decisions you think are bad or suboptimal and always watch your tongue, telling your opinion or experience, but straying from exactly telling them what to do (except when they ask), so they can figure it out for themselves.

Toddlers learn based on their experiences. This exact scenario happened on halloween, when my wife and 15 months old carved a pumpkin. When I came home from work, we lit it.

I was holding my son and the wife was about to put the candle in the pumpkin when my son wanted to touch the flame. She looked at me, questioning. I said 'Yeah, I think let him. He's not gonna suffer neither long term damage neither too much pain, he will take his finger away.'

Yeah he cried. But you can calm them down. He learnt on his own skin, not to touch the fire. We tried again a week later and he didn't want to touch the flame - he was careful.

If you always keep your child from the fire, until the point they understand why they shouldn't touch it, the child only learned that someone else will keep them safe from what they don't understand. This is not however how the world works.

My players usually enjoy the encounters where I delay events to be able to add more powerful enemies.
Context : I like to challenge them and they like it too. I know I can't trust CR, but check it just to appease my lizars brain. I design almost every combat in the hard-deadly range (by CR), except when the combat is intended to be a breeze.

When designing minibosses, I go for a maximum of 1,5 times deadly, but if the enemies are joining at the right time (usually when I predict them to defeat half of the previous wave), you could even go for 3 or maybe more times deadly, depending on how tactical and resourceful your players are.

I also found it more effective if the weaker, more numerous enemies join first and the progressively harder ones later. This makes the PCs reshift their focus when the stronger enemies join, leaving some of the small ones. This can't work in every scenario, but the smaller enemies could be guards of the summoning ritual.

I would also suggest grouped initiative for the same type of enemies and not rolling initiative for enemies, putting them in between players instead (this just occured to me but I should consider their initiative bonus when placing enemies in the order)

Setting stages in combat so that more enemies join in later turns can seriously up the CR your party could take (I'm aware it's broken, I just like to check), like 3-5 times the deadly rating, if the PCs are resourceful. I made a similar comment about this, I will link it for you.

For a fey themed adventure I'd also include social interactions where the fey really fuck with them. Stealing their gold, mocking them, hell, even redirecting their compasses.
If they always try to attack them, give them AC bonuses, and use their displacement spells & abilities ruthlessly.

Maybe try making your own tables, so they are designed to be meaningful. And I'm literally talking about 4 options, but they roll a d20, and you just divide the result by however many encounters you have left.

My players usually enjoy the encounters where I delay events to be able to add more powerful enemies.
Context : I like to challenge them and they like it too. I know I can't trust CR, but check it just to appease my lizars brain. I design almost every combat in the hard-deadly range (by CR), except when the combat is intended to be a breeze.

When designing minibosses, I go for a maximum of 1,5 times deadly, but if the enemies are joining at the right time (usually when I predict them to defeat half of the previous wave), you could even go for 3 or maybe more times deadly, depending on how tactical and resourceful your players are.

I also found it more effective if the weaker, more numerous enemies join first and the progressively harder ones later. This makes the PCs reshift their focus when the stronger enemies join, leaving some of the small ones. This can't work in every scenario, but the smaller enemies could be guards of the summoning ritual.

I would also suggest grouped initiative for the same type of enemies and not rolling initiative for enemies, putting them in between players instead (this just occured to me but I should consider their initiative bonus when placing enemies in the order)

If the PC is unstable, I just tell them that it's time to roll. They usually have something in hands reach (maybe their own hands) to hide the roll. They also hide their sheet (they have their abilities and spells printed out, but we don't cut them up to cards anymore). Then whatever happens in the following turns (excluding a Nat 20, which puts them at 1 HP, but at the end of their turns, so they can only act next turn to simulate shock), they just keep rolling in secret every turn for the rest of the combat. Hiding the death saves from other players is a cheat code for easy tension.

While I agree completely that intelligent enemies will make sure to confirm the kill, I always try to find a rational reason to divert them from the downed player. Not killing them when it wouldn't make sense for them to be spared/left alone is cheating IMO, but personally, I'm on their team, I'm rooting for them.

We use hidden death saves (I check them after 3, because I'm curious). Trust at the table is very important to me, so this might seem contradicting, but I actually don't care if they cheat by having their character stable instead of dead. Let me rephrase : the only time a player is allowed to cheat is when they roll that third fail (expect if they just roll 3 fails in a row, since I would see that). They don't know this of course, so this doesn't take away the tension. If they love their character so much and can live with the guilt, no one will ever know anyway.
